findings.quote: After eleven years of sitting in morning traffic behind a school bus,
findings.note: Fourteen words precede the main subject "I", a late subject.
The clause hides who should be doing the noting. The draft never names the actor, and the surrounding sentences do not identify one.

findings.quote: The combination was forgotten twice in the first week.
findings.note: The actor is not named in the clause or the surrounding sentences, though the context points to the narrator; the reader has to work it out.

findings.quote: bus routes are cleared first, by six in the morning
findings.note: The clause does not say who clears the bus routes; the snow contracts specify a schedule only, and no actor appears in the surrounding sentences. The reader needs that party to judge whether the schedule holds on the side streets too.

findings.quote: The decision to sell was made
findings.note: "decision" buries the verb "decide" behind "was made".
"evaluation" buries the verb "evaluate" behind "carried out".
"realization" is an action noun carried by the empty verb "come to"; the verb "realize" exists.
Doubled pair "plain and simple" says one thing twice; the comparison before it already conveys the same idea.
"picturesque" appears twice within two sentences; the first occurrence is "a picturesque row of Victorian houses".
"bike" repeats within three sentences; the first occurrence is in the preceding sentence, "My bike was stolen in June."

findings.quote: I reached the bottom of the hill by seven.
findings.note: "I left", "I reached" and "I arrived" form a three-sentence template of subject-verb-plus-time-marker clauses; the first occurrence is "I left the house at six-forty."

findings.quote: Municipal snow contracts in our city
findings.note: The sentence opens on municipal snow contracts, a new element; the previous sentence was about arriving at the desk with wet socks and a temper.

findings.quote: My bike was stolen in June.
findings.note: The sentence opens on "My bike", a new element; the previous sentence was about the Fenwick Road bridge and crossing it on foot. Nothing earlier in the paragraph prepares for the bicycle.

findings.quote: an anchor that kept me moored
findings.note: Mixed figure: the vehicle is first a cocoon, a thing that encloses, and within the same sentence an anchor with a mooring line, a thing that holds a vessel in place. The two images cannot both hold, and the draft never settles which relation to the car it means.
Stock simile that supplies no mechanism or picture beyond the literal claim that walking made the neighbourhood more legible. What a book opening has to do with streets is left unsaid.

findings.quote: It should be noted that I am not trying to tell anyone else how to live. Everyone's situation is different, and what works for one person will not necessarily work for another. Many people live too far from work, or have children to drop off, or have jobs that require a car, and I do not want to suggest that any of them are doing anything wrong.
findings.note: Stacked qualification: the disclaimer is hedged three times over — not telling anyone how to live, situations differ, not suggesting anyone is wrong.

findings.quote: I pass a picturesque row of Victorian houses on Linden Street, then the picturesque old mill that someone has turned into flats.
findings.note: Repeated example: a second sights-on-the-walk example built in the same "I pass... then..." form as the sentence it follows.
The reader cannot identify 'the hill' or 'that February' here; the paragraph beginning 'The first winter was very hard.' supplies the first winter and names Carver Hill.
The draft does not say who raised the concerns, and no nearby sentence identifies them.

findings.quote: It was decided in 2023 that all changes would go through this process
findings.note: The draft never says who decided that all changes would go through the board process. The surrounding sentences describe the board's routine, but none names the actor behind this decision.
"The board" opens three consecutive sentences. Because "board" is a noun rather than an article or pronoun, this counts as a run of three.

findings.quote: Given the results of the pilot and what both teams told us in the May retrospective,
findings.note: This opening places 16 words before the main subject "I".
"cumbersome" appears twice in this paragraph, with the first occurrence in the sentence about the checklist.
The word "approves" appears in the preceding sentence, so "Approvals" repeats the same root within two sentences.
"full and complete" is a doubled pair that says the same thing twice.

findings.quote: toll booth on the highway to production
findings.note: Stock image standing in for the argument; the draft never unpacks what the booth charges or who pays it, so it substitutes a picture for the reasoning. The surrounding sentences describe delay, not a toll.
"review" is an action noun carried by "conduct"; the verb "review" is buried.
"determination" carries the action while "makes" does the grammatical work; the verb root "determine" is available.
The noun "criticism" buries the verb "criticize" behind the weak "is".
Restatement: the pilot outcome was already given in "both teams cut their median wait from six days to under one, and neither shipped a change that had to be rolled back."
The paragraph reports results for 'the pilot' and 'both teams' before the draft names either; the pilot is identified only in the paragraph beginning 'In March and April, the Payments'.
The noun "decision" buries the verb "decide", carried by the empty verb "made".
"Undertaking" and "assessment" are action nouns; "given" and "carry out" carry no action, leaving the clause with no real actor.
"Assessment" is a noun burying the action; "carry out" is the weak verb.

findings.quote: In the weeks after the water went down and the loss adjuster had come round to photograph each and every room,
findings.note: The subject is preceded by 22 words. The main subject is Ellen.

findings.quote: Flood warnings for Quay Street were not issued
findings.note: The draft never says who failed to issue the warnings; that omission of an accountable body is central to the paragraph's point about the warnings coming late.
No promiser is named. The paragraph presents this as a broken commitment, so the missing actor is the party responsible for it.
Doubled pair: "each and every" says the same thing twice.
"sodden" appears in two consecutive sentences; the first is in "the smell of sodden flour".
Three consecutive sentences open with "She" plus a past-tense verb ("She rang", "She carried", "She went back"), and a fourth follows the same template with "She left".
"whole" appears twice in the first two sentences: "the whole street" and "the whole body".

findings.quote: affected many people on Quay Street in many different ways
findings.note: "affect" appears here and again as "affected" in the paragraph's final sentence; both lie within three sentences.

findings.quote: Some lost stock and some lost income, and some lost things
findings.note: Three consecutive clauses built on the same subject-verb-complement template with "some lost".
Stock image standing in for an argument the paragraph does not make: it asserts a general awakening for the street without saying who was woken or to what.

findings.quote: harder to put a price on
findings.note: Stock image standing in for the specific intangible losses the paragraph never names. The figure gestures at a category without supplying any content for it.

findings.quote: the beating heart of Quay Street
findings.note: Stock image. The figure substitutes for any account of what the bakery actually does for the street.

findings.quote: lit a fire under the council
findings.note: Stock image stacked on the wave of support in the same sentence. The draft leaves unspecified what support did and what the council then did.

findings.quote: The flood affected many people on Quay Street in many different ways. Some lost stock and some lost income, and some lost things that are harder to put a price on. It is difficult to overstate how much the flood affected the people of the street, and it would be impossible to describe every way in which their lives were changed by it.
findings.note: Restatement: three sentences that all assert the flood affected the street, repeating the point made in 'The flood affected many people on Quay Street in many different ways.'
The sentence opens on Tom, who appears nowhere in the paragraph; the previous sentences are about damage to the room. The link to the prior sentence, 'sodden', only arrives at the end of the clause.
The sentence opens on a general baking fact with no connection to the previous sentence about Tom driving for flour. Nothing earlier in the paragraph prepares this element.

findings.quote: The insurance payment, when it came in August
findings.note: This paragraph's August settlement and 'five months of lost trade' depend on the extent of the damage and the timeline the draft supplies only later, at 'The damage was really extensive' and 'Morrow's reopened on the first of October'.
This paragraph resumes the flood-morning account begun at 'At a quarter past four on the ninth of March', after the intervening paragraph about the August insurance payment.

findings.quote: The flood affected many people on Quay Street
findings.note: Restates the street-wide impact already asserted at 'It was obviously a shock to the whole street'; the added detail ('Some lost stock and some lost income') stays at the same level of generality.
"decision" names the action carried by the empty verb "made".
"Expectation" buries the act of expecting behind "There was".
"Observation" buries the act of observing behind "made".

findings.quote: It is a feeling that is familiar. It is a feeling that recurs.
findings.note: Two consecutive sentences built on the same template, with "It is a feeling that" repeated; the earlier occurrence is the first sentence of this pair.
The root "decid-" appears twice within one sentence; the first occurrence is "decided" at the start of the sentence.
"resolution" and the phrase "arrived at" repeat from the preceding sentence's "a resolution would be arrived at"; the second appearance falls within the paragraph.
"Feeling" appears three times within three sentences, first in the clause "with the feeling that nothing had been accomplished."
The draft never says who accomplished nothing or who failed to accomplish it; the passive hides the responsible party.

findings.quote: a resolution would be arrived at
findings.note: The clause does not say who would arrive at the resolution, and neither the surrounding sentences nor the paragraph names that actor.

findings.quote: It was decided by the committee that a decision
findings.note: The paragraph beginning 'It was decided by the committee that a decision' repeats the point of the earlier paragraph beginning 'It was decided by the committee thxt x determination'.

findings.quote: There was an expectation that a resolution
findings.note: The paragraph beginning 'There was an expectation that a resolution' repeats the point of the earlier paragraph beginning 'There was an expectation that'.

findings.quote: Some of us left the room with the feeling
findings.note: The paragraph beginning 'Some of us left the room with the feeling' repeats the point of the earlier paragraph beginning 'Some of us left the room with the feeling'.
